passage.excerpt: Marcion of Pontus succeeded [Cerdo] and developed his doctrine, blaspheming with shameless effrontery Him proclaimed as God by the law and the prophets, declaring Him the author of evils, taking delight in war, infirm of purpose, and contrary to Himself. But Jesus, derived from that father above the God who made the world, came into Judaea in the times of Pontius Pilate, was manifested in the form of a man — abolishing the prophets and the law — but not truly taking flesh. He also mutilated the Gospel according to Luke, removing all that is written respecting the generation of the Lord.

subject_entity.notes: Roman historical work by Tacitus used here for Nero and the fire/persecution context in Rome.

object_entity.notes: Roman senator and historian; author of the Annals and Histories. Annals 15.44 provides key external pagan witness to Christ and Nero's persecution.

evidence.notes: Tacitus names himself implicitly through his distinctive authorial voice; style universally identified as Tacitean.

passage.excerpt: To scotch the rumour, Nero substituted as culprits, and punished with the utmost refinements of cruelty, a class of men, loathed for their vices, whom the crowd styled Christians.
passage.notes: Tacitus records Nero's persecution of Christians after the Great Fire of Rome (64 AD).

subject_entity.notes: Anonymous apology c. 130-200 addressed to a pagan inquirer describing Christians as a third race living in the world but not of it; contains significant Logos theology.

object_entity.proposition_label: Christ the Logos is the pre-existent Son of God
object_entity.description: The Word/Logos of God, who became incarnate as Jesus Christ, pre-existed creation as the Son and mind of the Father, through whom all things were made.

evidence.notes: Diognetus 5-6 sojourner theology provides context for the Logos-driven Christian identity.

passage.excerpt: Christians are not distinguished from other men by country or language or customs. But while dwelling in Greek and barbarian cities, and following the local customs, they display to us their wonderful and confessedly striking method of life. They dwell in their own countries, but simply as sojourners. As citizens they share in all things, and yet endure all things as if foreigners. Every foreign land is to them as their native country, and every land of their birth as a land of strangers.
passage.notes: Christians as a distinct third people; resident aliens in every nation; sociological description of early Christianity

evidence.notes: Describes organized church community at Carthage with regular meetings and common fund

passage.excerpt: We are a body knit together by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope. We meet together as an assembly and a congregation. We pray together, we read scripture, we offer exhortation. Our presidents are elders, approved men. There is no buying and selling of any sort in the things of God. Even if there is a chest of sorts, it is not made up of purchase-money. On the monthly day, each puts in a small donation, if he will, and only if he be willing; for no one is compelled. These gifts are not spent on feasts or drinking bouts but to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined to the house.
passage.notes: Description of Christian assembly, common fund, and community life in Carthage
